extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor lawyers, courts, worker advocates, and others assessing worker classification under the FLSA
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the Fair Labor Standards Act using the economic-reality test and related statutory/textual principles. Applies the totality-of-the-circumstances approach and explains how courts and the Department weigh factors such as opportunity for profit or loss, investments, permanency, exclusivity, and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual scope of 'employee' under the FLSA / remedial purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act's definitions (including the 'suffer or permit' language) indicate broad coverage of who is an employee under the FLSA; the Department recognizes that the Act's remedial purpose and definitions support expansive coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encino addressed exemptions and rejected a blanket 'narrow construction' rule for exemptions, but did not change the Act's definitional text; courts may give a 'fair' reading but the inclusion of 'suffer or permit' shows Congress intended broad coverage (29 U.S.C. 203(g)). The Department will consider remedial purpose but rejects treating remedial purpose as an absolute rule that must always control the inquiry. See Encino Motorcars v. Navarro, 138 S. Ct. 1134 (2018) and discussion of pre-Encino case law (e.g., Rutherford, Rosenwasser).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic reality / totality-of-the-circumstances approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine status by applying an economic reality test that examines all relevant facts and circumstances to assess whether the worker is economically dependent on the employer (employee) or in business for themself (independent contractor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department use multiple factors as guides; none is dispositive. The overarching focus is economic dependence (see Flint Eng'g and related cases). Apply a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis rather than any single mechanical test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss based on managerial skill
rubrics_metrics.description: This factor weighs toward independent-contractor status to the extent the individual has an opportunity to earn profits or incur losses based on his or her exercise of initiative (such as managerial skill or business acumen or judgment) or management of his or her investment in or capital expenditure (e.g., helpers, equipment, materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted regulatory language: 'This factor weighs towards the individual being an independent contractor to the extent the individual has an opportunity to earn profits or incur losses based on his or her exercise of initiative (such as managerial skill or business acumen or judgment) or management of his or her investment in or capital expenditure on, for example, helpers or equipment or material to further his or her work.' (86 FR 1247). Consider evidence that a worker's technical proficiency translates into profit only if the worker can exercise managerial skill (marketing, advertising, communicating value to clients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the worker's investments (investments factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the worker's investments are capital or entrepreneurial in nature; such investments indicate independent-contractor status, whereas minimal or non-entrepreneurial investments point toward employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether investments are the kind of capital/entrepreneurial expenditures that show the worker is in business for themself (e.g., specialized equipment purchased for business use). Distinguish between an already-owned personal item used for work (less weight) and items purchased for a business purpose (can indicate entrepreneurial investment). Compare investments qualitatively to employer investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative investments comparison (qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the worker's investments to the employer's investments in its overall business on a qualitative basis rather than by dollar-for-dollar comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text and discussion instruct focusing on qualitative comparison of the nature and type of investments rather than raw dollar amounts or company size (29 CFR 795.110(b)(2)). Courts have considered relative investments, but district courts should not permit invasive discovery solely to elicit employer dollar amounts. The Department emphasizes qualitative assessment to avoid focusing on absolute size differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs unilaterally imposed by the potential employer
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account costs that are unilaterally imposed by the potential employer on the worker when evaluating the investments/opportunity-for-profit analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department modified the investments provision to add 'and costs that are unilaterally imposed by the potential employer on the worker.' Such costs may indicate employee status if the employer effectively transfers business costs to workers without the worker making independent business decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency of the working relationship (duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more permanent or long-term the relationship between the worker and the potential employer, the more it indicates employee status; short or discrete engagements are more consistent with independent-contractor status, subject to context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider total length of relationship, exclusivity, and whether continuous engagement is intrinsic to the industry (e.g., agriculture seasonality). Temporary or seasonal work may still be employee status if the permanency is effectively for the operative period or industry norms. Cases: Parrish, Capital Int'l, DialAmerica, Pilgrim Equip., Lauritzen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity as relevant to permanency and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusivity of the working relationship is a relevant consideration under the permanence and control factors, but exclusivity is not required to find employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusivity may inform conclusions about economic dependence and interacts with control (e.g., if employer practices preclude outside work). Courts consider exclusivity among other facts (Keller, Scantland, Hobbs). The Department notes exclusivity can be relevant under multiple factors consistent with totality-of-the-circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for industry-specific operational characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying the factors, make allowances for operational characteristics that are unique or intrinsic to a particular business or industry, which may affect how factors like permanency or investments are interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: temporary rig welders or seasonal agricultural workers—short duration may be intrinsic to the industry rather than an indicator of independent-contractor intent. Courts must account for industry norms so they do not misclassify workers because of atypical operational features (Mr. W Fireworks, Flint Eng'g, Superior Care).

rubrics_metrics.name: No single factor is dispositive; economic dependence is dispositive focus
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the enumerated factors alone determines the outcome; instead use them as guides, with the overarching inquiry being whether the worker is economically dependent on the employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple appellate decisions instruct that 'none of the factors alone is dispositive' and courts must weigh the totality of circumstances with ultimate focus on economic dependence (Flint Eng'g, Lauritzen, Pilgrim Equip.). Apply a balanced approach rather than treating any one factor as conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial skill and technical proficiency interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether technical proficiency actually translates into increased profit potential for the worker by virtue of managerial skill (e.g., marketing, advertising, client persuasion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted that technical proficiency alone is insufficient; the worker's ability to maximize profits from skill depends on managerial skill or ability to communicate/persuade clients. Examples like marketing/advertising are provided as illustrations of managerial skill relevant to the opportunity-for-profit analysis.
